discussion: What stood out in this chapter, and what surprised you?
What is the most interesting point? Do you find Bitcoin inspiring, and why?
Which points need further explanation? Select one critical issue from the chapter and explain it.
title: Bitcoin from first principles: chapter 1 of Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, and Bitcoin today

nodes.label: Money
nodes.body: Bitcoin is first of all money: a unit of account that is stored and transmitted among participants in the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Unit
nodes.body: The chapter's Introduction fixes the vocabulary before anything else, and the capital letter matters (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Bitcoin unit
nodes.body: The unit of currency is bitcoin with a small b, and the system is Bitcoin with a capital B, so a student who writes about both must keep the two apart (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: bitcoin with a small b, Bitcoin with a capital B
nodes.definition: The unit of currency is bitcoin with a small b; the system is Bitcoin with a capital B.

nodes.label: Supply
nodes.body: Bitcoin's supply follows a schedule written into the software rather than a decision by any authority (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Supply cap
nodes.body: The schedule creates bitcoin in eras of 210000 blocks, halving each time, so the sum of every subsidy is 20999999.9769 bitcoin - just below 21 million, as the chapter says (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
nodes.example: the sum of every block subsidy
nodes.definition: New bitcoin is created on a schedule that halves the subsidy every 210000 blocks, so the total supply stays just below 21 million.

nodes.label: Halving
nodes.body: The subsidy halved at block 840000 on 2024-04-20, after the book was published, to 3.125 bitcoin per block (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
nodes.definition: The block subsidy halves every 210000 blocks; after the halving at block 840000 on 2024-04-20 it is 3.125 bitcoin.

nodes.label: Price
nodes.body: The section Finding the Current Price of Bitcoin answers who sets the price: nobody does, markets do (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Floating exchange rate
nodes.body: Bitcoin has a floating exchange rate: its value moves with supply and demand in the markets where it is traded, and pricing services average those markets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The price of bitcoin is set by markets: a floating exchange rate that moves with supply and demand.

nodes.label: Issuance
nodes.body: The chapter explains who creates money in Bitcoin - no one, in the sense a central bank does (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Central bank replacement
nodes.body: Bitcoin mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank.

nodes.label: Deflation
nodes.body: With diminishing issuance the currency is deflationary over the long term, and after about 6.93 million blocks, around 2140, no new bitcoin is issued; at ten minutes a block that reaches about 2140.8 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Issuance diminishes, so the currency is deflationary; after about 6.93 million blocks, around 2140, no new bitcoin is issued.

nodes.label: Network
nodes.body: Bitcoin is also a network of participants that agree on transactions without a central authority (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Consensus
nodes.body: Consensus is the network's agreement about the state of transactions, reached without a trusted party (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Proof of work
nodes.body: Proof of work runs a global lottery every 10 minutes on average that lets the decentralized network reach consensus; it descends from Hashcash, which used costly computation to throttle abuse (Back, 2002).
nodes.example: a toy search for a hash starting with 0000
nodes.definition: Proof of work makes adding a block costly and easy to check; a toy version searches for a number whose SHA-256 hash starts with zeros.

io.code: next(n for n in range(10**6) if __import__('hashlib').sha256(f'SEN0401-{n}'.encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0000'))

nodes.label: Double-spend
nodes.body: Proof of work solves the double-spend, the weakness of earlier digital currencies that had been handled only by clearing every transaction through a central clearinghouse (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The double-spend problem - spending one unit twice - which Bitcoin's consensus solves without a central clearinghouse.

nodes.label: History
nodes.body: The History of Bitcoin section traces the system from a paper to a running network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Whitepaper
nodes.body: Bitcoin was first described in 2008 in Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, a paper written under the name Satoshi Nakamoto that proposes a purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash (Nakamoto, 2008).
nodes.example: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
nodes.definition: The 2008 paper by Satoshi Nakamoto that first described Bitcoin.

nodes.label: Reference implementation
nodes.body: The network started in 2009 from a reference implementation published by Nakamoto and revised since by many programmers; Bitcoin Core's releases page now lists 31.1 as its newest release (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.definition: The software Nakamoto published in 2009, since revised by many programmers; Bitcoin Core's newest listed release is 31.1.

nodes.label: Wallet
nodes.body: Getting Started turns to the wallet, the software through which people actually use Bitcoin, and Choosing a Bitcoin Wallet warns that the choice depends on use and expertise rather than any single brand (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Wallet platform
nodes.body: The section Types of Bitcoin wallets sorts wallets first by the platform they run on (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Desktop wallet
nodes.body: A desktop wallet was the first type of Bitcoin wallet, created as a reference implementation, and runs on general-purpose operating systems whose security is often weak (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The first type of Bitcoin wallet, run on a general-purpose operating system.

nodes.label: Mobile wallet
nodes.body: A mobile wallet is the most common type of Bitcoin wallet, running on smartphone operating systems such as iOS and Android (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The most common type of Bitcoin wallet, run on a smartphone.

nodes.label: Web wallet
nodes.body: Web wallets are accessed through a web browser, which makes them convenient and places trust in whoever runs the service (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A wallet used through a web browser.

nodes.label: Node type
nodes.body: The section Full node versus Lightweight sorts wallets by how much of the network's work they do themselves (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Full node
nodes.body: A full node validates the entire history of Bitcoin transactions itself, so it depends on nobody else for the truth of the ledger (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A program that validates the entire history of Bitcoin transactions itself.

nodes.label: Lightweight client
nodes.body: A lightweight client relies on other nodes for validation, trading some independence for convenience (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A client that relies on others for validation instead of checking every transaction itself.

nodes.label: Key control
nodes.body: The section Who controls the keys asks the question that decides who really owns the bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Noncustodial wallet
nodes.body: In a noncustodial wallet only the user holds the keys, so only the user can spend - and only the user can lose access (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A wallet where only the user holds the keys - who controls the keys controls the bitcoin.

nodes.label: Backup
nodes.body: Because the user holds the keys, the user must also be able to restore them, which is what the section Recovery Codes is about (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Recovery code
nodes.body: A recovery code is a list of words, numbers or letters chosen randomly by the wallet and used as the basis for its keys; the book's samples follow BIP 39, whose initial entropy is 128 to 256 bits (Palatinus et al., 2013).
nodes.definition: A recovery code of words, numbers or letters chosen by the wallet from which its keys are generated; the book's samples follow BIP 39.

nodes.label: Usage
nodes.body: The rest of the chapter follows Alice through Quick Start, Getting Your First Bitcoin, and Sending and Receiving Bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Address
nodes.body: The section Bitcoin Addresses explains what a user gives others in order to be paid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Bitcoin address
nodes.body: A Bitcoin address is derived from the user's private key and registered nowhere; sharing it lets others pay but never withdraw, and a new address for each invoice protects privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: an address shown as a QR code
nodes.definition: A number derived from the private key that others use to pay you; a new one per invoice protects privacy.

nodes.label: Transfer
nodes.body: Receiving Bitcoin and Sending and Receiving Bitcoin show the two directions of a payment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Sending and receiving
nodes.body: To receive, a wallet shows an address or invoice, often as a QR code; to send, the wallet signs a transaction spending to the recipient's address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Receiving shows an address or invoice; sending signs a transaction that spends to someone else's address.

nodes.label: Semantic bridge
nodes.body: The course theme of semantic technologies meets the chapter at its central idea: control by whoever holds the keys, without a central registry (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

nodes.label: Decentralized identity
nodes.body: W3C's Decentralized Identifiers apply that idea to identity, and Verifiable Credentials build signed claims on top of it, so a project can carry the chapter's key principle into semantic web standards (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025).
nodes.example: a DID controlled by its holder
nodes.definition: W3C Decentralized Identifiers apply the same principle to identity: control by whoever holds the keys, with no central registry.

nodes.label: Acquisition
nodes.body: Getting Your First Bitcoin warns that bitcoin transactions are irreversible, so sellers accepting reversible card payments verify buyers first (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Buy from friend
nodes.body: Finding a friend who has bitcoin and buying directly is the least complicated way to start (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The least complicated way to get a first bitcoin: buy directly from someone who has some.

nodes.label: Earn bitcoin
nodes.body: A programmer can sell programming skills and a hairdresser can cut hair for bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: payment for a product or service
nodes.definition: Earn bitcoin by selling a product or service for it.

nodes.label: Bitcoin ATM
nodes.body: A Bitcoin ATM accepts cash and sends bitcoin to a smartphone wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A machine that accepts cash and sends bitcoin to a smartphone wallet.

nodes.label: Currency exchange
nodes.body: Many countries have currency exchanges linked to bank accounts that swap bitcoin with local currency (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: an exchange linked to a bank account
nodes.definition: A currency exchange that swaps bitcoin with local currency.

nodes.label: Nature
nodes.body: Before the history, the chapter says what kind of thing Bitcoin is; the owner's course notes gather this into characteristics and architecture (Altunel, 2021).

nodes.label: Characteristic
nodes.body: The chapter's opening pages describe Bitcoin by four characteristics, drawn together as a set in the owner's course notes (Altunel, 2021).

nodes.label: Virtual
nodes.body: Bitcoin is entirely virtual: there are no physical coins, not even individual digital coins, because the coins are implied in transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: There are no physical coins, not even individual digital coins; coins are implied in transactions.

nodes.label: Borderless
nodes.body: Bitcoin is fast, secure and borderless, which makes it arguably the perfect form of money for the internet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Fast, secure and borderless - arguably the perfect form of money for the internet.

nodes.label: Decentralized
nodes.body: Bitcoin is decentralized by design, free of any central authority or point of control that can be attacked or corrupted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Free of any central authority or point of control that can be attacked or corrupted.

nodes.label: Robust
nodes.body: A decentralized currency was needed to be robust against intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Built to withstand intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements.

nodes.label: Architecture
nodes.body: Behind the scenes, the chapter lists four parts Bitcoin consists of, one of which - proof of work - appears under consensus (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Peer-to-peer protocol
nodes.body: The Bitcoin protocol is a decentralized peer-to-peer network, so no server sits at the centre (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The Bitcoin protocol: a decentralized peer-to-peer network.

nodes.label: Public journal
nodes.body: The blockchain is a public transaction journal that anyone can read and verify (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A public transaction journal: the blockchain.

nodes.label: Consensus rule set
nodes.body: The consensus rules are a set of rules for independent transaction validation and currency issuance (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A set of rules for independent transaction validation and currency issuance.
